Behind a shop door in Beijing, there's a staircase. It leads to a city built to hide six million people.
Nineteen sixty-nine. Chinese and Soviet troops clash on a frozen border. Beijing fears nuclear war.
Mao's order: dig tunnels deep, store grain everywhere.
Over three hundred thousand people start digging. Students too. Some by hand.
Ten years later: tunnels up to eighteen meters deep, under eighty-five square kilometers.
Around ninety secret entrances, hidden inside shops.
Down here: clinics, schools, cinemas, a roller rink, even a mushroom farm.
The plan: half the city goes underground. The rest flees to the hills.
Rumors say the tunnels reach Zhongnanhai, where China's leaders work. That has never been confirmed.
But people did move in. By twenty fifteen, about two hundred eighty thousand lived in Beijing's basements and shelters.
And the digging never stopped. Chinese rules still require shelters under many new buildings.
In two thousand eight, state TV even showed the army's own tunnels: reportedly about five thousand kilometers.
Built for a war that never came. So why does China keep building underground?
